rule: Features placed low on the head and gathered together read younger and cuter; raising the eye line makes a face read adult.
On a teen face the jaw (eyes to chin) grows to about half the face; on children it is shorter. A longer lower face reads older.
Both eyes share the same tilt, the same shape, the same level, and equal distance from the nose and from the face edge.
The top eyelid is always darker and heavier than the bottom one.
A round eye becomes an oval only where perspective demands it (head tilted or turned); the pupil on a tall-oval eye stays a circle.
On a pretty young face the top lip is horizontal or curves slightly down; the smile curve is carried by the bottom lip and small upturned creases at the corners.
In an open-mouth smile, the more teeth that show, the more intense the laughter reads.
Nose, mouth and ears stay small so the eyes dominate the face.
A few clear head planes look sharp; too many planes make the head needlessly complicated.
